title: The Town Where You're Not Allowed to Die: The True Story
description:
In 1998, scientists from four countries dug up seven coal miners buried in the Arctic, hoping the 1918 flu was still frozen inside them. It wasn't. The man who actually found the virus had done it a year earlier, in Alaska, with his wife's garden shears. And the town those miners are buried in hasn't buried a coffin since 1950.

This is the true story behind "the town where it's illegal to die": Longyearbyen, Svalbard.

Facts used: Longyearbyen is named after John Munro Longyear of Boston, whose Arctic Coal Company founded Longyear City in 1906; Store Norske bought it in 1916. The steamship Forsete arrived from Tromsø on September 24, 1918, and seven young miners, aged 19 to 28, died in the first week of October; the frozen ground was blasted with dynamite for their graves. In 1998 Kirsty Duncan's team from Canada, Britain, the United States and Norway found the coffins less than one meter down, above the permafrost, which started at about 1.2 meters. The flu virus was first isolated in 1933. Johan Hultin dug at Brevig Mission, Alaska, in 1951 and failed to grow the virus; in 1997, aged 72, after reading Jeffery Taubenberger's paper in Science, he went back, found "Lucy" with her lungs preserved, and mailed the tissue to Taubenberger's lab. Scientists rebuilt the 1918 virus in a secure lab in 2005. Longyearbyen stopped coffin burials in 1950; it has no delivery room, and dying there is not actually illegal.
